title: Silk Hidden in 8,500-Year-Old Graves
text: Silk thread rots fast, so how do you prove people had it 8,500 years ago? Scientists scooped soil from under the pelvis of skeletons in three Neolithic graves at Jiahu and tested it for proteins. Two graves held traces of silkworm fibroin, the protein that makes silk. A bone needle lay in one of them, and rough weaving tools turned up across the site.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Biomolecular Evidence of Silk from 8,500 Years Ago

title: A 5,500-Year-Old Shoe Stuffed with Grass
text: In 2008, archaeologists in a dry Armenian cave found a leather shoe more than 5,500 years old. It was cut from a single piece of cowhide, laced with a leather thong, and stuffed with loose grass, perhaps to hold its shape. About a modern European size 37, it was worn on someone's right foot. It lay upside down in a pit, under a broken pot, beside goat horns.

source.name: PLOS ONE: First Direct Evidence of Chalcolithic Footwear from the Near Eastern Highlands

title: Sea-Snail Purple in a Copper Camp
text: At Slaves' Hill, a copper-smelting camp in the desert of southern Israel, archaeologists found scraps of wool dyed true purple. Chemical tests traced the colour to Mediterranean sea snails, so the cloth had travelled inland from the coast. Dated to around 1000 BCE, they are the oldest true purple textiles known from the southern Levant, and they were lying among the smelting waste.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Early evidence of royal purple dyed textile from Timna Valley (Israel)

title: Sagebrush Sandals Under Volcanic Ash
place: Fort Rock Cave, Lake County, Oregon, USA
text: In 1938, Luther Cressman dug nearly 100 sandals made of sagebrush bark out of Fort Rock Cave. They lay beneath ash from the eruption that created Crater Lake, and radiocarbon dating later showed they were made about 10,250 to 9,300 years ago. Sizes range from big adults to small children. Many are worn through at the heel, and one pair has tiny scorch marks.

source.name: University of Oregon: Focus on Footwear

title: The Mill Girls Walk Out
text: In February 1834, Lowell's cotton-mill owners cut wages by 12.5 percent. When they fired a worker named Julia Wilson, she gave the signal by waving her calash headdress, and about 800 young women walked out. They paraded through town calling themselves 'daughters of freemen.' They lost, but in 1836 up to 2,000 struck again, and several companies backed down.

source.name: National Park Service: Labor Reform, Early Strikes (Lowell National Historical Park)

title: Phoenix Boots Fit for the Liao Court
text: These tall boots come from the Liao, a dynasty that ruled northern China from 907 to 1125. Their outer silk is kesi, a tapestry weave, showing pairs of phoenixes chasing a flaming pearl among clouds, with two kinds of metal thread. Tailors cut the cloth so a pearl sits right at the shin, the calf and the instep. Liao emperors even sent kesi robes to the Song emperor as gifts.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Boot (Liao dynasty)

title: Birds for Scholars, Beasts for Soldiers
text: In 1391, new Ming clothing rules ordered court officials to wear decorated squares showing their rank: birds for civil officials, animals for military ones. These rank badges were sewn to the front and back of robes, and an official's wife wore badges matching her husband's. Later Qing badges showed the creature facing a sun, which stood for the emperor, as a sign of loyalty.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Rank Badge (buzi)

title: Edo Firefighters in European Wool
text: Edo was a crowded city of wooden houses, so fires broke out often. Firefighters wore protective jackets of leather or wool, and the wool came all the way from Europe. One late-1700s suit, now in Cleveland, carries a white crest of three interlocking rings inside a tortoise-shell frame, telling everyone which house its wearer served. Uniform, armour and badge, all in one outfit.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Firefighter's Suit (Kaji shozoku)

title: Crocodiles and Kings on Sumba Cloth
text: On the Indonesian island of Sumba, mantles called hinggi were worn at ceremonies and given as required gifts at births, marriages and deaths. Their patterns are dyed into the cotton threads before weaving, a method called ikat. This one shows an open shellfish and crocodiles, both signs of royal power, plus standing men in horned headdresses, a motif going back to Neolithic times.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Hinggi

title: Ship Cloths for Life's Big Crossings
text: For several hundred years, cloths called tampan pasisir played a part in nearly every ritual in southern Sumatra. This one shows a ship, woven with extra threads into a cotton base. No written myths explain these cloths, so their exact meaning is lost, but the ship may stand for safe passage from one stage of life to the next. Cloths this old rarely survive Indonesia's tropical climate.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Tampan Pasisir (Ship Cloth)

title: Spirit Patterns in Abacá Thread
text: The Mandaya people of southeastern Mindanao weave a cloth called dagmay, not from cotton or silk but from abacá fibres stripped by hand. Before weaving, chosen threads are bound tightly so the dye cannot reach them, leaving patterns that appear as the cloth grows on the loom. The designs carry Mandaya ideas about protection, fertility and the umagad, or ancestral spirits.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Mandaya ikat textile (dagmay)

title: Ten Metres of Cloth, 320 Grams
text: Dhaka was famous for cotton muslin so fine it sold across India and the Middle East. From the late 1700s it also became the fabric of choice in Britain and France for white, high-waisted dresses, worn with Kashmir shawls. A length made around 1855, now in London's V&A, is about 10 metres long yet weighs only 320 grams, and is decorated with delicate chikan embroidery.

source.name: V&A: Chikan Embroidered Muslin

title: A Shawl That Maps a City
text: Kashmir's famous shawls were made of pashmina, fine goat hair. Around 1870, embroiderers in Srinagar made one that was never meant to be worn: a map of their own city, stitched so finely it looks woven. Dal Lake, the Jhelum River, a fort and the main mosque appear among many little buildings, and a haloed man in a boat may be Maharaja Ranbir Singh.

source.name: V&A: Map shawl of Srinagar

title: Bukhara's Blazing Silk Ikats
text: In 19th-century Bukhara, wealthy townspeople hung dazzling silk ikat panels in their reception rooms. Every colour meant binding the warp threads tightly and dyeing them before weaving, which gives the patterns soft, 'fuzzy' edges. This hanging, joined from five loom widths in five colours, shows amulets and palmettes. It dates from the early 1800s, among the earliest known Central Asian ikats.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Wall Hanging (pardah)

title: Gold Letters on Yemen's Flame Cloth
text: Ikat means dyeing threads in patterns before they are woven. The name is a Malay word, yet it may have begun in South Arabia, and Yemeni ikats from the 900s are among the oldest known. This cotton cloth from Sanaa has 'flame' patterns and a Kufic inscription in gold leaf naming the Zaydi imam Yusuf ibn Yahya. One phrase, 'to God,' sits upside down.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Ikat tiraz

title: Silver-Threaded Kaftans for Sultans
text: In the late 1500s, Ottoman silk weaving reached its height. Imperial kaftans covered in big medallions of flowers and leaves, including some worn by young princes, are still kept in Istanbul's Topkapı Palace. A length from one such kaftan, now in Cleveland, glitters with silver thread. It uses lampas, two weaves combined in one cloth to give two contrasting surfaces.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Brocaded silk with foliate medallions from a kaftan

title: Hands, Birds and Knives in Kente
place: Ewe weaving country, Volta Region, Ghana
text: This Ewe-style kente cloth from Ghana or Togo was woven as one long strip, then cut into twenty pieces and sewn together by hand. Extra weft threads form tiny pictures: hands, birds, insects, knives, combs and four-legged animals. An important man wore it on special occasions, wrapped around his waist and tossed over his shoulder, its colours and patterns announcing his wealth.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Prestige cloth (kete or kente)

title: A Rainbow from a Few Dye Pots
text: A woollen curtain from 6th-century Antinoë in Egypt shows a saddled horse galloping inside a ring of hearts. Its many shades came from just a few dyes, often the costliest part of making cloth: an insect red, perhaps Armenian cochineal; indigo blue; yellow and brown from fustic trees; green from fustic plus indigo; and a purple mane from madder mixed with indigo.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Curtain Fragment with Galloping Horse

title: A Silk Cap Praising the Sultan
text: In medieval Egypt, a man's outfit wasn't complete without headwear. This 14th-century silk cap was woven with stripes of prancing animals, crescent moons and Arabic words: 'Glory to our lord Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir.' Such caps came from tightly regulated workshops in Cairo. Mamluk rulers gave lavish garments as tokens of honour, and the cap's pale pink trim may once have been bold red.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Cap with Striped Inscribed Silk

title: Madagascar's Silk Turns White
text: Across much of Madagascar, people of every age and class wore the lamba, an untailored wrap. Merina weavers made splendid ones from shining silk, decorated with floating-thread motifs called akotifahana. White had once been the colour of commoners and enslaved people, but when Christianity became the state religion in 1869, elite churchgoers chose white silk lambas. Knotted fringes copied Chinese-made 'Manila shawls.'

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Wrapper (Lamba Akotifahana)

title: The Diné Dress That Protects
text: Diné (Navajo) weaver D. Y. Begay says every Diné woman should own a biil'éé, a woven dress that holds spiritual power and gives protection. This wool example from the early 1880s is two matching tapestry-woven panels joined at the sides and shoulders, a style that grew out of one-piece dresses in the late 1700s. It could be cinched with a woven belt or a silver concha belt.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Woman's Two-Piece Dress (Biil'éé)

title: Ninety-Six Panels of Macaw Feathers
text: In the ancient Andes, cloth covered in feathers was among the most prized luxuries. This panel probably came from an offering on Peru's far south coast: over half a dozen big ceramic vessels shaped like people, buried with 96 rolled panels inside. Each was covered in blue-and-yellow macaw feathers, knotted onto strings and stitched to cotton. Ties suggest they were hung up to make a space radiant.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Feathered Panel

title: Tunics Woven by the Chosen Women
text: In the Inca Empire, finely woven tapestry tunics were a privilege of nobles. Some were made by noblewomen and professional weavers, others by the Aclla, or Chosen Women, who lived in cloistered communities, brewing beer and weaving fine cloth for the state. The state handed tunics out as prized gifts to loyal allies. This one carries the 'Inca Key,' one of the commonest tunic patterns.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Tunic (Inca)

title: A Chief's Feather Cloak Flies Home
text: In January 1779 at Kealakekua Bay, the chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu gave Captain Cook the feathered cloak he was wearing, the ʻahu ʻula, together with his feathered helmet. The cloak used feathers from about 20,000 birds. After passing through English collections, it reached New Zealand's national museum in 1912. In March 2016 it flew home to Hawaiʻi, and in 2020 it was returned for good.

source.name: Te Papa: Feather cloak and helmet gifted to Captain Cook to return permanently to Hawaiʻi

source2.name: Te Papa: Te Papa to return treasures gifted to Captain Cook to Hawaiʻi

title: The Loom That Read Punched Cards
text: Joseph Marie Jacquard of Lyon made weaving complex cloth such as damask far simpler. His loom, first shown in 1801, read thousands of punched cards laced together, each row of holes matching one row of the pattern. Charles Babbage later borrowed the idea to program his Analytical Engine. By the 1820s Scottish weavers used Jacquard looms for Paisley shawls and Dunfermline damask.

source.name: National Museums Scotland: The Jacquard loom, innovation in textiles and computing

source2.name: Science Museum Group: Joseph Marie Jacquard
